title: Jesus Looked Around the Table and Said, “One of You Will Betray Me.” Suddenly Everyone Started Asking the Same Question.
paragraphs: Jesus Looked Around the Table and Said, “One of You Will Betray Me.” Suddenly Everyone Started Asking the Same Question.
The Betrayer Revealed — and the terrifying question the disciples asked before anyone dared accuse somebody else.
There was bread on the table.
A cup.
Men who had walked dusty roads together.
Men who had watched demons flee, storms become still, blind eyes open, crippled bodies rise, and grieving families receive their dead back alive.
And somewhere at that table sat a traitor.
He did not look like one.
That may be the most disturbing part.
Judas Iscariot was not standing outside the room wearing the face of an enemy. He was reclining near Jesus with the others.
Close enough to eat with Him.
Close enough to hear His voice.
Close enough to receive bread from His hand.
And yet his heart was already moving toward betrayal.
Then Jesus spoke.
Matthew records His words in Greek:
“Ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι εἷς ἐξ ὑμῶν παραδώσει με.”
Literally:
“Truly I tell you, one of you will hand Me over.”
One of you.
Imagine what happened to that room.
Conversations died.
Hands stopped moving.
Eyes lifted from the table.
The men who had been eating beside Jesus suddenly realized that the greatest threat in the room was not outside the door.
It was sitting among them.
But then something happened that should haunt every Christian who has ever become more skilled at detecting another person's sin than examining his own heart.
The disciples did not immediately begin pointing fingers.
They began asking questions.
About themselves.
Matthew 26:22 preserves the question:
“Μήτι ἐγώ εἰμι, κύριε;”
“Mēti egō eimi, Kyrie?”
“Surely it is not I, Lord?”
Read that again.
Not:
“Lord, is it Peter?”
Not:
“Is it Matthew?”
“Is it Thomas?”
“I always suspected Judas.”
No.
“Surely it is not I, Lord?”
Suddenly every man at the table was forced to look somewhere most of us desperately try to avoid.
Inside.
And perhaps that is where this story stops being about Judas for a moment and starts becoming painfully personal.
Because it is easy to read the Bible already knowing who the villain is.
We know Judas betrays Jesus.
We know the silver.
We know the kiss.
We know Gethsemane.
We know how the story ends.
So we can sit safely on the other side of two thousand years, point toward Judas, and whisper:
“How could you?”
But Scripture does not give us that luxury.
Before the betrayer is fully exposed, the question echoes around the table.
“Is it I?”
And maybe before asking how Judas could betray Jesus, we need enough courage to ask where our own hearts have betrayed Him.
Have I confessed Christ with my mouth while negotiating with sin in private?
Have I worshiped on Sunday and deliberately ignored Him on Monday?
Have I wanted Jesus as Savior but resisted Him as Lord?
Have I learned Christian vocabulary while slowly losing Christian tenderness?
Have I condemned sins I can see in other people while protecting the ones nobody can see in me?
Have I become comfortable sitting near Jesus while refusing to surrender something to Jesus?
That is where this story becomes uncomfortable.
Because proximity to holy things is not the same thing as surrender to Christ.
Judas had extraordinary proximity.
He heard teachings from Jesus Himself.
He witnessed miracles.
He traveled with the Twelve.
He participated in their shared ministry.
He occupied a trusted position involving the common money bag, according to John’s Gospel.
He sat at the final meal.
And still...
his heart was not right.
That should destroy one of Christianity's most dangerous illusions:
“I am around Christian things, therefore everything between God and me must be fine.”
You can know worship songs and still need repentance.
You can quote Scripture and still conceal bitterness.
You can post verses and still harbor secret compromise.
You can serve in ministry and still need your heart searched.
You can know what Christians say without truly surrendering what Christ asks.
None of those observations means every struggling believer is another Judas.
Far from it.
Peter failed catastrophically too.
Before sunrise, Peter would deny Jesus three times.
Yet Peter's story would not end in denial.
That distinction matters enormously.
The Gospel is not teaching that one failure automatically makes someone Judas.
It is showing us something much deeper about the human heart, sin, repentance, and grace.
Judas betrayed.
Peter denied.
Both sinned terribly.
But Peter would eventually be broken, restored, recommissioned, and sent to feed Christ's sheep.
Failure does not have to become your final chapter.
This is why the Gospel is not merely a warning about betrayal.
It is an invitation to come out of hiding.
Maybe you have betrayed your own confession more times than you want to remember.
Maybe there are things on your phone you would panic if someone discovered.
Maybe bitterness has lived in you so long that you have renamed it “discernment.”
Maybe your marriage sees a version of you your church never sees.
Maybe you have been pretending to be spiritually alive while privately wondering when your heart became this cold.
Maybe nobody knows.
Jesus does.
And that truth can either terrify you...
or become the beginning of your freedom.
Because the Jesus at this table is not confused.
He is not discovering Judas's betrayal in real time.
He knows.
Matthew records Jesus saying that the Son of Man goes “as it is written of Him,” while also pronouncing a dreadful warning concerning the betrayer.
Human evil is real.
Human responsibility is real.
And yet human betrayal does not overthrow the sovereign redemptive purpose of God.
Judas is not stronger than Jesus.
The conspiracy is not stronger than Jesus.
The soldiers will not be stronger than Jesus.
Pilate will not be stronger than Jesus.
The nails will not be stronger than Jesus.
The tomb will not be stronger than Jesus.
The scandal will not have the last word.
Grace will.
But we need to be precise about how the betrayer is revealed, because the Gospel accounts give us details that become even more powerful when we do not flatten them into one scene.
In Matthew 26, after the disciples ask, “Surely it is not I, Lord?” Jesus speaks about the one dipping his hand with Him in the dish.
Then Judas asks a question of his own.
His wording is striking.
“Μήτι ἐγώ εἰμι, ῥαββί;”
“Surely it is not I, Rabbi?”
Notice the difference Matthew records.
The other disciples had addressed Jesus as “Lord.”
Judas says, “Rabbi.”
Teacher.
Jesus answers him:
“Σὺ εἶπας.”
“You have said it.”
But John's Gospel takes us even closer.
John 13 says Jesus became troubled in spirit and testified that one of them would betray Him.
The disciples looked at one another, uncertain whom He meant.
Peter motioned to the disciple whom Jesus loved to ask Jesus who it was.
Jesus answered that it was the one for whom He would dip the morsel and give it to him.
Then Jesus dipped the morsel.
And gave it to Judas.
Do not rush past that.
The hand Judas would betray was still extending something toward him.
The Lord knew what Judas was about to do.
And Judas was still close enough to receive from His hand.
Then comes one of the darkest sentences in the New Testament.
John 13:27:
“καὶ μετὰ τὸ ψωμίον τότε εἰσῆλθεν εἰς ἐκεῖνον ὁ Σατανᾶς.”
“And after the morsel, then Satan entered into him.”
Jesus tells Judas:
“What you are doing, do quickly.”
And Judas leaves.
John adds a tiny sentence.
Three Greek words:
“ἦν δὲ νύξ.”
“Now it was night.”
Of course it was.
Night outside.
Night inside.
A man walked away from the Light of the world and disappeared into darkness.
Yet even here we should resist adding something Scripture does not say.

John tells us that Jesus gave the identifying sign concerning the morsel, but the other disciples still did not understand why Judas left. Some thought Jesus had instructed him, because Judas kept the money bag, to buy what was needed for the feast or give something to the poor.
Think about that.
Even when Judas walked out, they apparently did not all comprehend what was happening.
The betrayer had hidden well.
Sin often does.
It learns vocabulary.
It learns appearances.
It learns when to smile.
It learns how to survive around holy people without surrendering to a holy God.
And that is why the question at the table matters so much.
“Is it I?”
There are moments when mature faith stops saying, “God, show me what is wrong with everybody else,” and begins praying something closer to David's prayer in Psalm 139:
Search me.
Know me.
Test me.
See whether there is a grievous way in me.
Lead me.
That prayer is dangerous because God may answer it.
He may expose the resentment you have justified.
The secret habit you have minimized.
The pride you disguised as confidence.
The envy you called ambition.
The unforgiveness you renamed boundaries.
The lukewarmness you blamed entirely on exhaustion.
The compromise you promised yourself was temporary.
But when Jesus exposes something, the answer is not to run deeper into darkness.
Bring it into His light.
This is where Judas's story should drive us not toward hopelessness, but toward Christ.
Because somewhere reading this is a person thinking:
“If people knew what I have done, they would never look at me the same.”
Maybe.
People are people.
But salvation was never built upon people knowing the polished version of you.
It was built upon Jesus Christ knowing the worst truth about sinners and going to the cross anyway.
The Gospel does not say your sin is small.
It says Christ is sufficient.
It does not say rebellion does not matter.
It says there is forgiveness for those who turn to Christ.
It does not tell you to decorate your chains.
It calls you out of them.
Repentance is not pretending the darkness never happened.
Repentance is turning from darkness toward the One who is Light.
Grace is not God announcing that sin never mattered.
Look at the cross.
Sin mattered enough that the sinless Son of God suffered for sinners.
Grace means that Christ bore what guilty people could never erase by religious performance.
He was betrayed.
Arrested.
Rejected.
Mocked.
Scourged.
Crucified.
And He rose.
The cross appeared to be scandal.
God turned it into the proclamation of grace.
What looked like the triumph of darkness became the place where Christ bore sin.
What looked like the end became the road toward resurrection morning.
That is why your darkest chapter does not have to be your final chapter either.
Not because you can rewrite yourself.
Because Jesus Christ saves sinners.
Because Jesus restores the repentant.
Because Jesus still calls people out of darkness.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe the most important question you can ask tonight is not:
“Who is Judas in my life?”
Maybe it is:
“Lord... is there something in me that I have been refusing to surrender?”
Do not answer quickly.
Sit there for a moment.
“Μήτι ἐγώ εἰμι, κύριε;”
“Surely it is not I, Lord?”
If your conscience immediately brought something to mind, do not scroll fast enough to silence it.
Bring it to Jesus.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Ask for mercy.
Seek reconciliation where reconciliation is biblically possible.
Ask another mature believer for help if you need accountability.
There is no spiritual prize for becoming excellent at hiding.
Christ did not call you to manage darkness.
He called you into light.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to tell strangers every private detail. But you can make one honest declaration.
Someone reading the comments may realize they are not the only believer fighting a private battle.
Someone may finally ask for prayer.
Someone may finally repent.
Someone may finally come home.
And if you know a Christian who has slowly become cold, send this to them without condemnation.
Sharing the Gospel cannot save us.
Jesus saves us.
But saved people have beautiful reasons to tell others about the Savior.

So if you want your Facebook presence to glorify God, consider using it deliberately for Christ. Let truth travel farther than gossip. Let grace travel farther than scandal. Let the name of Jesus appear in places where despair has been getting all the attention.
There may come a night when the question is no longer theoretical.
When temptation is loud.
When your heart is cold.
When you need to remember three words:
“Is it I?”
And then three more:
“Come to Jesus.”
It does not.
It cannot.
Not because you must give money to earn grace.
You cannot.
Grace cannot be bought.
More importantly, your support helps us keep pointing people beyond merchandise, beyond personalities, beyond algorithms, and back toward Jesus Christ.
Not for guilt.
Not for applause.
Not to prove your Christianity.
Tell them about Jesus.
Tell them repentance is still possible while there is breath to turn to Him.
Tell them grace is not permission to remain in darkness.
Tell them forgiveness was purchased at an immeasurable price.
Tell them the cross is stronger than their shame.
Tell them the empty tomb means darkness does not get the final sentence.
And before you leave this table...
ask the question.
Not about your spouse.
Not about your pastor.
Not about the politician you cannot stand.
Not about the Christian who disappointed you.
Not about Judas.
About you.
“Μήτι ἐγώ εἰμι, κύριε;”
“Lord... is it I?”
And when Jesus puts His finger on the place you hoped He would overlook, do not run into the night.
Run toward Christ.
Because the most frightening thing about Judas was not merely that he fell.
It was that he walked away from Jesus into the darkness.
You do not have to.
Come into the light.
Come with the failure.
Come with the shame.
Come with the secret.
Come repentant.
Come believing.
Come to the crucified and risen Christ.
And when grace has found you there, do not keep the story to yourself.
Follow.
Invite someone else closer to the truth.
Support Gospel work if God has given you the desire and means to do so.
But above everything else...
follow Jesus.
Because one day nobody will care how convincing your Christian appearance was.
Only whether you truly belonged to Christ.
And perhaps that is the line worth carrying with you long after this article disappears from your screen:
Do not become so comfortable sitting at the table with Jesus that you stop asking whether your heart still belongs to Him.
